title: Binary Classification
subtitle: Topic: Binary Classification · Subject: Supervised Machine Learning. Three beginner, two medium and two advanced questions; seven distinct instructional diagrams; balanced choices and beginner-friendly explanations.
hero:
BINARY CLASSIFICATION · VISUAL STUDY

Learn two-class decisions from labeled examples

A binary classifier distinguishes two outcomes, predicts a score or probability, and applies a decision threshold. Confusion-matrix metrics and careful evaluation reveal the consequences of its mistakes.

questions.stem: What is Binary Classification in supervised machine learning, and how are labeled training examples used to predict one of two possible outcomes?
options: Binary classification groups unlabeled examples into two clusters based on similarity, then assigns class names afterward. Its training stage does not need target labels, since the groups define themselves from the feature values.

Binary classification learns from examples with features and one of two target labels, such as fraud or legitimate. It uses learned patterns to predict the class or positive-class probability for previously unseen examples.

Binary classification predicts a continuously varying numerical target and rounds the result into two classes only for reporting. Target labels are optional because the model's main objective is to estimate real-valued quantities accurately.

Binary classification learns a separate probability for every possible class in a large class catalog, then selects two outcomes after training. Its labels must represent more than two mutually exclusive categories during model fitting.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Binary classification is supervised learning with two possible target classes. Training examples contain features and known outcomes, such as fraudulent or legitimate transactions. The model learns how features relate to those labels and applies that knowledge to unseen cases. It may output a predicted class directly or a probability used to make the decision. For example, a bank can use transaction amount, timing, and permitted context to predict whether a new payment is suspicious. The true fraud label is the training target, not an input feature.

questions.tag: Beginner · Sigmoid probability and decision threshold
questions.stem: How does a Binary Classification model turn a score into a class prediction, and why can changing a probability threshold alter its decisions?
options: A binary classifier always treats raw model scores as probabilities, even when they are negative or greater than one. The decision threshold changes the model's learned weights automatically rather than only its predicted labels.

A binary classifier uses the same threshold for every application because 0.5 is mathematically optimal. Adjusting it changes the meaning of the positive label but cannot alter which examples receive positive predictions.

A binary classifier must first convert probabilities to hard labels during model fitting, then use those labels as scores for prediction. Threshold adjustments are possible only by retraining the complete model with different labels.

A binary classifier can map a score through sigmoid to estimate class-1 probability, then predict positive if it meets a chosen threshold. Changing that threshold alters decisions without necessarily retraining the underlying model.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Logistic regression can calculate a real-valued score and turn it into a probability using sigmoid. A decision threshold converts that probability into a hard label. At threshold 0.5, a probability of 0.82 predicts positive, while 0.35 predicts negative. Raising the threshold may reduce false alarms but can also miss positives. For example, an email filter might use a conservative threshold before automatically blocking messages. The classifier's underlying scores can stay unchanged while the decision policy changes.

QUESTION 02 · BINARY CLASSIFICATION

A classifier such as logistic regression maps a score to the positive-class probability. The decision threshold then determines which class label to output.

questions.tag: Beginner · TP, TN, FP and FN
questions.stem: What do true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives mean in a Binary Classification confusion matrix?
options: True positives and true negatives are correct positive and negative predictions; false positives are negative cases predicted positive, while false negatives are positive cases predicted negative. The counts summarize different error types.

True positives are cases where both labels are zero, while true negatives are cases where both labels are one. False positives and false negatives depend only on the model's confidence, not on actual labels.

True positives are all examples with high predicted probability, regardless of their real labels, and true negatives have low scores. False positives are uncertain cases and false negatives are examples excluded from training.

True positives and false positives count only the real positive examples; true negatives and false negatives count only the real negatives. Prediction labels matter only after those actual-label totals have been calculated.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A confusion matrix compares predicted labels with actual labels. True positives (TP) correctly find positives, and true negatives (TN) correctly reject negatives. False positives (FP) are false alarms, while false negatives (FN) are missed positives. In the diagram, there are 25 TP, 60 TN, 10 FP, and 5 FN out of 100 cases. Imagine checking manufactured products for defects: an FP rejects a good item, while an FN lets a defective item pass. These error types can have very different consequences.

questions.tag: Medium · Precision, recall, accuracy and F1
questions.stem: How are precision, recall, accuracy, and F1 calculated from a Binary Classification confusion matrix with TP=25, FP=10, FN=5, and TN=60?
options: Precision is TP divided by all actual positives, giving 83.3%, while recall is TP divided by predicted positives, giving 71.4%. Accuracy is 85%, and F1 is calculated from the true negatives alone.
Precision is 25/35=71.4%, recall is 25/30=83.3%, and accuracy is 85%. F1 instead equals the arithmetic mean of precision and recall, giving about 77.4% for these counts.
Precision is 25/(25+10)=71.4%, recall is 25/(25+5)=83.3%, accuracy is (25+60)/100=85%, and F1 is 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN)≈76.9%. These metrics reveal different kinds of performance.

Precision and recall both equal total correct predictions divided by 100, or 85%, because binary classification has only two classes. F1 is therefore always the same as accuracy for any binary confusion matrix.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are correct: 25/(25+10)=71.4%. Recall is the fraction of real positives found: 25/(25+5)=83.3%. Accuracy counts all correct cases: (25+60)/100=85%. F1 combines precision and recall using their harmonic mean, about 76.9%. For a quality-control model, higher recall catches more defective products, while higher precision reduces unnecessary rejections. Evaluating only accuracy hides which type of mistake the classifier makes.

questions.stem: How can Binary Classification be implemented in scikit-learn without fitting preprocessing on held-out data, and how should confusion-matrix metrics be calculated?
options: Standardize all available examples first and then split into training and test data. Train logistic regression on the training rows and select the best threshold by repeatedly checking test precision and recall.

Split labeled data, fit StandardScaler and LogisticRegression inside a training pipeline, and obtain positive-class probabilities on held-out examples. Apply a fixed threshold and calculate confusion matrix, precision, and recall using the true test labels.

Train logistic regression on the entire dataset, then create a test split only to calculate metrics. A pipeline prevents leakage even when its scaler and classifier have already been fitted to the test examples.

Split labeled examples, fit a scaler independently on the test data, and train logistic regression on scaled training examples. Different scaler estimates ensure that the test set is independent of learned training preprocessing.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Split data before fitting preprocessing or the classifier. A scikit-learn Pipeline fits StandardScaler only on training features and then trains LogisticRegression. On the holdout, the pipeline applies the already-fitted training scaler. Use predict_proba for scores, a fixed threshold for labels, and the confusion matrix to measure mistakes. The reproducible example trains on 135 cases and tests on 45. It produces TN=13, FP=9, FN=2, TP=21, precision 70.0%, and recall 91.3%. No threshold is tuned on test data.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 05 · BINARY CLASSIFICATION
scikit-learn · logistic regression holdout 15 lines
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, precision_score, recall_score
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=180, n_features=4,
    n_informative=3, n_redundant=0, random_state=7)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25,
    stratify=y, random_state=11)
m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr)
pred = (m.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1] >= .5).astype(int)
cm = confusion_matrix(yte, pred)
print(cm.tolist(), round(precision_score(yte,pred), 3),
      round(recall_score(yte,pred), 3))

With 135 training and 45 held-out cases, this 15-line scikit-learn pipeline produces TN=13, FP=9, FN=2, TP=21; precision 0.700 and recall 0.913.

questions.stem: Why can accuracy be misleading for imbalanced Binary Classification, and how do thresholds and precision-recall evaluation help reveal the trade-offs?
options: Accuracy becomes more reliable as the positive class gets rarer, because predicting the majority class is usually correct. A precision-recall curve adds little information unless positive and negative examples occur equally often.

Raising the threshold always increases precision and recall together, because fewer low-confidence positives are accepted. ROC and precision-recall curves therefore show the same fixed relationship for every binary classifier.

Accuracy reveals the rates of both missed positives and false alarms automatically, even with severe class imbalance. Once a model reaches high accuracy, changing the threshold cannot improve its practical usefulness.

An imbalanced dataset can produce high accuracy by mostly predicting the common class while missing rare positives. Thresholds change the precision-recall balance; PR curves can be especially informative when positives are uncommon.
questions.explanation: Explanation: If only 1% of transactions are fraudulent, always predicting legitimate gives 99% accuracy but catches no fraud. Precision tells how many predicted positives are correct; recall tells how many actual positives are found. Different thresholds change the trade-off, although precision is not guaranteed to increase every time the threshold rises. In the six-example diagram, raising the threshold improves precision from 66.7% to 100% but lowers recall from 66.7% to 33.3%. Precision-recall curves are especially informative for rare positives.

For six labeled scores, threshold 0.50 gives precision and recall 66.7%; threshold 0.75 gives precision 100% but recall 33.3%.

questions.stem: How should a Binary Classification system be evaluated and deployed to avoid data leakage, choose an appropriate decision threshold, and monitor changing real-world behavior?
options: Fit preprocessing and the classifier on training data, select thresholds and evaluate calibration on validation data, then use an untouched test set for final evaluation. After deployment, monitor drift and error costs over time.

Fit preprocessing on the complete dataset to stabilize statistics, then train the model on one subset. Adjust thresholds on the test set until accuracy is highest and reuse those test results as an unbiased final estimate.

Select the decision threshold after deployment using every future prediction as ground truth, without collecting confirmed outcomes. A model's confidence scores remain calibrated automatically when customer behavior or class frequencies change.

Train and select thresholds using only test examples so deployment conditions are represented accurately. Once the model produces probability-like numbers, calibration, monitoring, and group-aware evaluation no longer affect reliability.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Keep training, validation, and test roles separate. Fit preprocessing and classifier weights on training data, then use validation examples to select thresholds and evaluate whether scores are calibrated. Reserve the test set for final evaluation after those choices. Split by customer, time, person, or group when related records might otherwise leak. Following deployment, monitor changes in class balance, calibration, and the costs of false alarms or missed positives. For example, fraud-detection performance may drift as payment habits change. Confidence alone is not proof of calibration.
